stops.name: Stuttgart: Wilhelm Hauff turns the case into a novella
stops.campa: Nearly a century on, the Swabian poet Wilhelm Hauff writes his novella 'Jud Süß,' fixing the hanged financier into German letters as a figure of legend: the Jew who rose too high and was cast down. The trial records lie in the archives, contradictory and vague; but the story escapes the records. From here the memory of Joseph Süß ceases to be history and becomes a mask that each age will put on for its own purposes, dark and light by turns.

stops.name: Munich: Lion Feuchtwanger redeems the man in a novel
stops.campa: The Jewish writer Lion Feuchtwanger publishes his great novel 'Jud Süß,' making of the financier not a villain but a tragic and humane figure who, at the end, chooses his people and his faith over life: a meditation on power, identity, and the outsider destroyed by the state he served. It becomes a world bestseller, staged and filmed. In Feuchtwanger's telling the scapegoat is given back his dignity and his inwardness, the truth the trial denied him. For a moment the slander is answered.

stops.name: Berlin: the Nazi film weaponizes the name
stops.campa: The regime turns the story into its opposite. Veit Harlan's 'Jud Süß,' commissioned by Goebbels, premieres: a lavish, poisonous inversion that makes of Oppenheimer a lecherous, scheming demon, and of his execution a righteous purge. Millions are made to watch it; it is shown to SS units before their killings. The two-century afterlife of a slander reaches its nadir: the murdered Court Jew, scapegoat of 1738, is disinterred to serve as the pretext for a genocide. The cage on the Prag has cast a longer shadow than any who raised it could have dreamed.
